learn.hook: India's general election is one of the biggest events organised anywhere on Earth: polling teams carry machines by road, boat and on foot so that even remote voters can vote!
points: India is divided into areas called constituencies. The Lok Sabha has 543 constituencies, and each elects one Member of Parliament (MP). Each state is also divided into assembly constituencies that elect MLAs. Elections are normally held every 5 years.
Every citizen aged 18 or above whose name is on the electoral roll (voter list) can vote. Voting is secret, and an indelible ink mark on the finger helps prevent anyone voting twice.

The Election Commission of India (ECI), set up on 25 January 1950 under Article 324 of the Constitution, is an independent body that conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.

Main steps: dates are announced and the Model Code of Conduct begins, candidates file nominations, nominations are checked, campaigning takes place, people vote on polling day, and votes are counted and results declared.
Votes are cast on Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs). A VVPAT machine prints a slip showing the chosen symbol so the voter can check it. NOTA ('None of the Above') lets a voter reject all candidates.
Some constituencies are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes: only candidates from these groups can contest there, but all voters of the constituency vote.

example.q: Think it through: Why is voting in India kept secret?
steps: If others could see how someone voted, powerful people could threaten or bribe voters.
Secrecy lets every voter choose freely, without fear of their boss, neighbours or even family.
This protects the freedom and fairness of the election.
example.answer: Secret voting protects voters from pressure and fear, so that every vote is a free choice.

learn.reallife: National Voters' Day is celebrated on 25 January, the day the Election Commission was set up. Ask an adult at home to show you the voter ID card (EPIC) and the ink mark after voting.

games.title: Steps of an election
games.prompt: Arrange the steps of an election from first to last
items: Election dates announced and Model Code of Conduct begins
Candidates file nomination papers
Nomination papers are checked (scrutiny)
Parties and candidates campaign
Voters cast their votes on polling day
Votes are counted and results declared

items.q: Normal term of the Lok Sabha (years)?
Year the Election Commission was set up?
First Chief Election Commissioner of India?

quiz.q: Which body conducts elections to the Lok Sabha?
quiz.explain: The Election Commission of India conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. State Election Commissions conduct panchayat and municipal elections.
steps: Asked: who conducts Lok Sabha elections.
The Election Commission of India conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President and Vice-President.
State Election Commissions conduct panchayat and municipal elections, so they do not fit.
So the answer is the Election Commission of India.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Election Commission of India with State Election Commissions or the courts

quiz.q: What does a VVPAT machine do?
options: Counts the population of a constituency
Prints a slip showing the symbol the voter chose, so the voter can check it
quiz.explain: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) shows a printed slip of the chosen symbol for a few seconds so the voter can verify the vote.
steps: Asked: what a VVPAT does.
Votes are cast on the EVM.
The VVPAT prints a slip showing the chosen symbol so the voter can check the vote.
It does not count votes, print ID cards or decide the winner.
Answer: Prints a slip showing the symbol the voter chose, so the voter can check it
quiz.mistake: Thinks VVPAT is the voting or counting machine itself

quiz.q: What is the Model Code of Conduct?
options: A law that sets the voting age
Guidelines that parties, candidates and governments must follow during elections
A list of all voters in a constituency
A rule for how to design an EVM
quiz.explain: It is a set of guidelines from the Election Commission. For example, the government should not announce new schemes to win votes once elections are announced.
steps: Asked: the meaning of the Model Code of Conduct.
It begins when election dates are announced.
It is a set of guidelines that parties, candidates and governments must follow during elections.
It is not the voter list or the law on voting age.
Answer: Guidelines that parties, candidates and governments must follow during elections
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Model Code of Conduct with the electoral roll or election laws

quiz.q: What does pressing NOTA on an EVM mean?
options: The voter supports the ruling party
The voter wants the election cancelled immediately
The voter rejects all the candidates
quiz.explain: NOTA stands for 'None of the Above'. It lets a voter record that they do not support any candidate. It was added in 2013 after a Supreme Court judgment.
steps: Asked: what pressing NOTA means.
NOTA stands for 'None of the Above'.
It lets a voter reject all the candidates.
It does not cancel the election or count for any party.
Answer: The voter rejects all the candidates
quiz.mistake: Thinks NOTA cancels the election or counts for some party

quiz.q: In a constituency reserved for Scheduled Castes, who can vote?
options: All registered voters of that constituency
quiz.explain: Reservation decides who can contest, not who can vote. Only Scheduled Caste candidates can stand, but every registered voter there votes.
steps: Asked: who votes in an SC-reserved constituency.
Reservation decides who can contest: only SC candidates can stand there.
All registered voters of the constituency still vote.
So reservation does not limit who can vote.
Answer: All registered voters of that constituency
quiz.mistake: Thinks a reserved seat also limits who can vote

quiz.q: What is an electoral roll?
options: The list of people eligible to vote in a constituency
quiz.explain: The electoral roll, or voter list, contains the names of all eligible voters. It is updated regularly.
steps: Asked: the meaning of electoral roll.
The electoral roll is the voter list.
It lists all people eligible to vote in a constituency.
It is not a list of candidates, results or parties.
Answer: The list of people eligible to vote in a constituency
quiz.mistake: Confuses the voter list with a list of candidates or results

quiz.q: Why is indelible ink put on a voter's finger?
options: To stop the same person from voting twice
To show which party the person voted for
quiz.explain: The ink mark cannot be removed easily for many days, so polling staff can see that the person has already voted.
steps: Asked: why indelible ink is put on a voter's finger.
The mark cannot be removed easily for many days.
So polling staff can see who has already voted, which stops voting twice.
It does not show the voter's choice; voting is secret.
Answer: To stop the same person from voting twice
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ink reveals the voter's choice, which would break secrecy

quiz.q: The Election Commission of India was set up on 25 January of which year?
quiz.explain: It was set up on 25 January 1950, a day before the Constitution came into force. National Voters' Day is celebrated on this date.
steps: Asked: the year the Election Commission was set up.
It was set up on 25 January 1950 under Article 324.
That is a day before the Constitution came into force; 1947 is independence.
Answer: 1950
quiz.mistake: Links the Election Commission with Independence Day (1947) or the first elections (1951–52)

teach.ask: Gappu waves a tiny flag: 'Who runs elections in India, and what happens from the announcement to the result?'
teach.praise: Super! The Election Commission runs it, adults of 18+ on the voter list vote secretly on EVMs, and then the votes are counted. Hooray for elections!
teach.nudge: Who organises the election? And what are the steps between announcement and the results?

revise.summary: India is divided into constituencies; the Lok Sabha has 543, each electing one MP, normally every 5 years. Citizens aged 18+ on the electoral roll vote secretly on EVMs with VVPAT. The independent Election Commission of India, set up on 25 January 1950, conducts elections.
focus: Role of the Election Commission of India and the steps of an election
EVM, VVPAT, NOTA, indelible ink and the electoral roll
Reserved constituencies: who can contest and who can vote
remember: Lok Sabha: 543 constituencies, one MP each; elections normally every 5 years
Election Commission of India: set up 25 January 1950 under Article 324
VVPAT prints a slip of the chosen symbol; NOTA = None of the Above
Reserved seats: only SC/ST candidates contest, but all voters of the constituency vote
traps: Don't confuse the Election Commission of India with State Election Commissions
A reserved seat does not limit who can vote
Indelible ink does not reveal the voter's choice

learn.hook: In a race, the runner who crosses the line first wins, even if just by a step. India's Lok Sabha elections work in a similar way!
points: First-Past-The-Post (FPTP): the country is divided into constituencies, each electing one representative. The candidate with the most votes wins, even with less than half of all votes.
Under FPTP, a party's share of seats can be very different from its share of votes, because only the winner in each constituency gets the seat.

Proportional Representation (PR): a party gets seats in proportion to its share of votes. In list PR, used in countries such as Israel and the Netherlands, votes are counted for parties, and each party's seats are filled from its list of candidates.

India uses FPTP for Lok Sabha and state Vidhan Sabha elections. It uses PR by single transferable vote (voters rank candidates by preference) to elect Rajya Sabha members (by MLAs), the President and the Vice-President.
India chose FPTP for direct elections because it is simple for voters, gives every area its own representative, and usually produces clear results and stable governments.

example.q: Think it through: In a constituency, Asha gets 42,000 votes, Bilal 38,000 and Charan 20,000 (total 1,00,000). Who wins under FPTP, and did the winner get a majority?
steps: Under FPTP, the candidate with the highest number of votes wins.
Asha has the most votes (42,000), so Asha wins the seat.
42% is less than half, so 58% of voters chose someone else, yet Asha still wins.
example.answer: Asha wins with 42% of the votes, which is the most votes but not a majority.

learn.reallife: When results are shown on TV, the Lok Sabha seat count of a party is often very different from its percentage of votes. That is FPTP at work.

games.title: FPTP or PR?
items: The candidate with the most votes wins the seat
Lok Sabha elections in India
Each constituency elects exactly one representative
State Vidhan Sabha elections in India

quiz.q: In a constituency, Asha gets 42,000 votes, Bilal 38,000 and Charan 20,000. Who wins under FPTP?
options: Nobody, because no one got more than half
quiz.explain: Under FPTP the candidate with the most votes wins. A majority (more than half) is not needed.
steps: Given: Asha 42,000, Bilal 38,000, Charan 20,000.
Rule: under FPTP, the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority.
Asha has the most votes.
So Asha wins; more than half is not needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks FPTP requires the winner to get more than 50% of votes

items: Asha
Bilal
Charan

quiz.q: In the same contest (42,000 + 38,000 + 20,000 votes), what percentage of the votes did the winner get?
quiz.explain: 42,000 out of 1,00,000 votes is 42%. So the winner won with less than half of the votes.
quiz.mistake: Adds the losers' votes (58%) or assumes the winner must have 50%

items: Asha
Bilal
Charan

quiz.q: A legislature has 200 seats and uses pure proportional representation. A party wins 25% of the votes. About how many seats should it get?
quiz.explain: Under PR, seats follow vote share: 25% of 200 = 50 seats.
quiz.mistake: Takes the percentage itself as the number of seats
steps: = 50 seats

quiz.q: Which elections in India are held using the First-Past-The-Post system?
quiz.explain: Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections use FPTP. The President, Vice-President and Rajya Sabha members are elected by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
steps: Asked: which Indian elections use FPTP.
FPTP is used for Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections.
President, Vice-President and Rajya Sabha use PR by single transferable vote.
So the answer is Lok Sabha elections.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all Indian elections use the same system

quiz.q: How is the President of India elected?
options: By an electoral college through proportional representation by single transferable vote
Directly by all voters through FPTP
quiz.explain: Elected MPs and elected MLAs form the electoral college, and they vote using the single transferable vote, a form of PR.
steps: Asked: how the President is elected.
An electoral college of elected MPs and elected MLAs votes.
They use proportional representation by single transferable vote.
So the President is not elected directly by all voters.
Answer: By an electoral college through proportional representation by single transferable vote
quiz.mistake: Assumes the President is chosen directly by the people like an MP

quiz.q: What is a major drawback of the FPTP system?
options: It is too complicated for voters to understand
A party's share of seats can be much larger or smaller than its share of votes
It needs the whole country to be one constituency
quiz.explain: In FPTP only the winner in each constituency gets the seat, so votes for losing candidates do not turn into seats.
steps: Asked: a major drawback of FPTP.
Under FPTP only the winner in each constituency gets the seat.
Votes for losing candidates do not turn into seats.
So a party's seat share can be very different from its vote share.
Answer: A party's share of seats can be much larger or smaller than its share of votes
quiz.mistake: Confuses the features of FPTP with those of list PR

quiz.q: Why did India choose FPTP for Lok Sabha elections?
options: It guarantees that every party gets seats equal to its votes
It is simple for voters and gives each area its own representative
It was required by the British Parliament
It removes the need for an Election Commission
quiz.explain: FPTP is easy to understand, links each constituency with one accountable representative, and tends to give clear results.
steps: Asked: why India chose FPTP for Lok Sabha.
FPTP is simple for voters.
It gives every area its own representative and usually clear results.
It does not give seats equal to votes; that is PR.
Answer: It is simple for voters and gives each area its own representative
quiz.mistake: Thinks FPTP gives perfectly proportional results, which is a feature of PR

quiz.q: Which country uses proportional representation with the whole country treated as one constituency?
quiz.explain: In Israel, seats in its parliament are shared out among parties according to their national vote share. India, the UK and Canada use FPTP for their national parliament elections.
steps: Asked: a country using PR with the whole country as one constituency.
In list PR, used in Israel, seats are shared by national vote share.
India, the UK and Canada use FPTP for national elections.
So the answer is Israel.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that the UK and Canada, like India, use FPTP

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'What is the difference between FPTP and proportional representation? Which one does India use?'
teach.praise: Now I see! In FPTP the top vote-getter wins; in PR seats follow vote share. India uses FPTP for the Lok Sabha and PR for the Rajya Sabha and President!
teach.nudge: You explained one system. What about the other, and where does India use each one?

revise.summary: Under First-Past-The-Post, each constituency elects one member and the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority. Under proportional representation, parties get seats in proportion to their votes. India uses FPTP for Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections.
focus: Find the FPTP winner and the winner's vote share
Work out seats under pure PR from vote share
Which Indian elections use FPTP and which use PR
remember: FPTP: most votes wins; a majority is not needed
PR: seats in proportion to vote share (e.g. 25% of 200 seats = 50)
India: FPTP for Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha; PR by single transferable vote for Rajya Sabha, President, Vice-President
List PR is used in countries such as Israel and the Netherlands
traps: Don't think the FPTP winner must get more than 50%
Don't take the vote percentage itself as the number of seats
The President is not elected directly by the people

learn.hook: For about 21 months, from 1975 to 1977, many rights that Indians took for granted were suspended. Then voters had their say at the ballot box. This chapter of our history shows why democratic safeguards matter.
points: The Constitution allows a national emergency under Article 352 when the country faces a grave threat. During an emergency, the central government gets extra powers and some fundamental rights can be suspended.

Background: on 12 June 1975, the Allahabad High Court declared Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's 1971 election from Rae Bareli void. At the same time, a large opposition movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan was demanding her resignation.

On 25 June 1975, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed a national emergency on the grounds of 'internal disturbance', on the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The government said this was needed to maintain order and stability.

During the Emergency, many fundamental rights were suspended, newspapers were censored, many opposition leaders and others were detained without trial, and elections were postponed. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made many changes to the Constitution.

Lok Sabha elections were held in March 1977. The ruling Congress lost, and the Emergency was withdrawn on 21 March 1977. The Janata Party formed the government, and Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress Prime Minister.

The 44th Amendment (1978) added safeguards: 'internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion', the President can declare an emergency only on the written advice of the Cabinet, and the rights in Articles 20 and 21 (including life and personal liberty) cannot be suspended.

example.q: Think it through: What lessons did India's democracy learn from the Emergency?
steps: It showed that the emergency powers in the Constitution could be used to suspend rights for a long time.
It showed how important a free press, independent courts and the right to protest are in a democracy.
In 1977, voters used their vote to change the government peacefully.
Parliament then passed the 44th Amendment so that emergency powers would be harder to misuse.
example.answer: Rights need strong safeguards, citizens and institutions must stay alert, and elections let people change governments peacefully.

learn.reallife: Whenever people discuss press freedom, the independence of courts or limits on government power, the experience of 1975–77 is often remembered.

games.title: Emergency timeline
games.prompt: Arrange the events from earliest to latest
items: Allahabad High Court verdict on the Rae Bareli election (June 1975)
Emergency proclaimed (25 June 1975)
42nd Amendment passed (1976)
Lok Sabha elections held (March 1977)
Morarji Desai becomes Prime Minister (March 1977)
44th Amendment adds safeguards (1978)

games.title: True or false?
items: The Emergency of 1975 was proclaimed on the grounds of 'internal disturbance'.
That was the ground given in 1975. The 44th Amendment later replaced it with 'armed rebellion'.
During the Emergency, newspapers faced censorship.
Newspapers had to get some news approved by censors before printing it.
The 1975 Emergency lasted for about five years.
It lasted about 21 months, from June 1975 to March 1977.
In the 1977 Lok Sabha elections, the party in power at the Centre lost.
The Janata Party won, and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister.
Today, a national emergency can be declared only on the grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
After the 44th Amendment (1978), these are the only grounds under Article 352.
The right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) can still be suspended during an emergency.
The 44th Amendment made sure Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an emergency.

quiz.q: On which date was the national emergency proclaimed in 1975?
quiz.explain: The Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court had given its verdict on the Rae Bareli election.
steps: Asked: the date the Emergency was proclaimed.
On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court declared the Rae Bareli election void.
The Emergency was proclaimed later, on 25 June 1975.
So the answer is 25 June 1975.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the High Court verdict date with the date the Emergency was proclaimed

quiz.q: Who was the President of India who proclaimed the Emergency in 1975?
quiz.explain: President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
steps: Asked: the President who proclaimed the Emergency.
On 25 June 1975, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed it.
He acted on the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
Answer: Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
quiz.mistake: Remembers a President from a nearby period but not the one in office in 1975

quiz.q: Under which Article number of the Constitution can a national emergency be proclaimed?
quiz.explain: Article 352 deals with a national emergency. Article 356 is about President's Rule in a state and Article 360 about financial emergency.
steps: Asked: the Article for a national emergency.
Article 352 deals with a national emergency.
Article 356 is President's Rule in a state; Article 360 is financial emergency.
So the answer is 352.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the national emergency with President's Rule (Article 356) or financial emergency (Article 360)

quiz.q: Which of these happened during the Emergency of 1975–77?
options: The first general elections were held
Newspapers were censored and many opposition leaders were detained
quiz.explain: Press censorship and detention of opposition leaders without trial were major features of the Emergency.
steps: Asked: what happened during the 1975–77 Emergency.
Rights were suspended, newspapers were censored and opposition leaders were detained without trial.
The Constitution (1950) and first elections (1951–52) came much earlier.
Answer: Newspapers were censored and many opposition leaders were detained
quiz.mistake: Mixes up events from different periods of Indian history

quiz.q: Who led the large opposition movement in 1974–75 that demanded the Prime Minister's resignation?
quiz.explain: Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) led the movement. Ambedkar, Patel and Rajendra Prasad had passed away before the 1970s.
steps: Asked: who led the 1974–75 opposition movement.
The movement demanding the PM's resignation was led by Jayaprakash Narayan.
Ambedkar, Patel and Rajendra Prasad had died before the 1970s.
Answer: Jayaprakash Narayan
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous national leader without checking the time period

quiz.q: What was the result of the Lok Sabha elections of March 1977?
options: The Janata Party formed the government and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister
The ruling party won every seat
The President dissolved all political parties
quiz.explain: Voters defeated the ruling Congress. The Janata Party formed the first non-Congress government at the Centre, led by Morarji Desai.
steps: Asked: the result of the March 1977 elections.
The ruling Congress lost.
The Janata Party formed the government and Morarji Desai became PM.
He was the first non-Congress Prime Minister.
Answer: The Janata Party formed the government and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister
quiz.mistake: Does not realise the 1977 elections changed the government

quiz.q: What change did the 44th Amendment (1978) make to emergency provisions?
options: It allowed emergencies to be declared without any reason
'Internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion' as a ground
It made the President directly elected
quiz.explain: The 44th Amendment narrowed the grounds to war, external aggression or armed rebellion, and added other safeguards.
steps: Asked: the 44th Amendment's change to emergency provisions.
The 44th Amendment (1978) added safeguards.
It replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground.
So it limited emergency powers; it did not widen them.
Answer: 'Internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion' as a ground
quiz.mistake: Thinks the amendment increased emergency powers rather than limiting them

quiz.q: About how long did the Emergency of 1975–77 last?
quiz.explain: It lasted from 25 June 1975 to March 1977, which is about 21 months.
steps: Given: from 25 June 1975 to 21 March 1977.
June 1975 → June 1976 = 12 months; June 1976 → March 1977 = 9 months.
12 + 9 = 21 months.
So it lasted about 21 months.
quiz.mistake: Does not work out the period from June 1975 to March 1977

teach.ask: Gappu looks worried: 'What was the Emergency, and what did India change afterwards so it would not happen the same way again?'
teach.praise: Thank you! In 1975 rights were suspended and the press censored, voters changed the government in 1977, and the 44th Amendment added safeguards. Lesson learnt!
teach.nudge: When did it happen, and what happened to people's rights? How did it end, and what safeguards came later?

revise.summary: On 25 June 1975, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed a national emergency under Article 352 on PM Indira Gandhi's advice. Rights were suspended, the press censored and opposition leaders detained. In 1977 voters defeated Congress; the 44th Amendment added safeguards.
focus: Background: Allahabad High Court verdict (12 June 1975) and the JP movement
The 1977 election result and the 44th Amendment safeguards
remember: Emergency proclaimed 25 June 1975; withdrawn 21 March 1977 (about 21 months)
Article 352: national emergency. 356: President's Rule. 360: financial emergency.
1977: Janata Party formed government; Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress PM
44th Amendment (1978): 'armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance'; Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended
traps: Don't mix up 12 June 1975 (court verdict) with 25 June 1975 (Emergency proclaimed)
Don't confuse Article 352 with Article 356 or 360
The 44th Amendment limited emergency powers; it did not increase them
